draft.title: The unreliable narrator
card: A narrator is the voice that tells the story. An unreliable narrator cannot be fully trusted to tell it truthfully or completely.
A narrator can be unreliable in three ways. They may lie, they may misunderstand what is happening, or they may leave things out.
Readers spot this through clues. Look for the narrator contradicting themselves, other characters reacting differently, or events that do not match what the narrator claims.
Writers use this to make readers look past what the narrator says and work out the truth for themselves. It can build suspense or show what the narrator is really like.
draft.remember: An unreliable narrator may lie, misunderstand or leave things out, so readers must look past their words.

opts: One who misunderstands what is happening
One who tells the story in the first person
One who describes a setting in detail
One who tells the story in past tense
a.why: An unreliable narrator cannot be fully trusted, and misunderstanding events is one way this happens. Using the first person, detail or past tense does not make a narrator untrustworthy.
a.clue: Which one makes the narrator's account wrong or incomplete?

b.q: Tom says he is the best player on his team and never makes mistakes. His teammates groan when he misses an easy goal. What does this suggest?
opts: Tom may be an unreliable narrator
Tom is a reliable narrator because he is confident
The teammates are the unreliable narrators
The story is told in non-standard verse
b.why: The teammates' reactions do not match Tom's claims, which is a clue that he cannot be fully trusted. Confidence does not make a narrator reliable. The reader must look past his words.
b.clue: Compare what Tom says with what others do.

a.best: One who misunderstands what is happening

b.best: Tom may be an unreliable narrator

problems.detail: The scenario never says Tom is the narrator. 'Tom says' reads like a character's speech, so students may not see why narrator reliability applies. State that Tom narrates the story, e.g. 'Tom narrates: I am the best player…'.
The right option is the only one with a hedge ('may'), so it stands out from the flat claims in the other options and could be picked without knowing the idea.

proposal.title: The unreliable narrator
card: A narrator is the voice that tells the story. An unreliable narrator cannot be fully trusted to tell it truthfully or completely.

A narrator can be unreliable in three ways: they may lie, misunderstand what is happening, or leave things out. Telling the story as I, or in past tense, does not make a narrator unreliable on its own.
Readers spot this through clues. Look for the narrator contradicting themselves, other characters reacting differently, or events that do not match what the narrator claims.
Writers use this to make readers look past what the narrator says and work out the truth for themselves. It can build suspense or show what the narrator is really like.
proposal.remember: Test the narrator's words against the clues around them, and trust the clues when the two clash.

b.q: Tom narrates a story about his soccer team. He tells readers he is the best player and never makes mistakes. Later he misses an easy goal, and his teammates groan. What does this suggest?
opts: Tom is unreliable, as his claims clash with events
Tom is reliable, as he speaks with confidence
The teammates are unreliable, as they groan at him
Tom is reliable, as he narrates in the first person
b.why: Tom is the narrator, and the missed goal and the teammates' groans do not match his claims. That clash is a clue he cannot be fully trusted. Confidence does not make a narrator reliable, and the teammates are not narrating at all.
b.clue: Compare what Tom tells readers with what actually happens.
